No. 26A382
In the Supreme Court of the United States
SAMUEL STRULOVITCH, MS ACQUISITION I, LLC, AND 10 CLAREMONT AVENUE, LLC,
Applicants,
v.
MOSHE BAIN,
Respondent,
and
PARKVIEW OPERATING CO., LLC, WESTCHESTER GARDENS REALTY LLC,
JONATHAN BLEIER, AND ROBERT BLEIER,
Nominal Respondents.
On Emergency Application for a Stay Pending Appellate Review
BRIEF AMICUS CURIAE OF
THE BECKET FUND FOR RELIGIOUS LIBERTY
IN SUPPORT OF APPLICANTS
WILLIAM J. HAUN
 Counsel of Record
MARK L. RIENZI
REBEKAH P. RICKETTS
HANNAH S. WANDER
THE BECKET FUND FOR 
 RELIGIOUS LIBERTY
1919 Pennsylvania Ave. NW
 Suite 400
Washington, D.C. 20006
(202) 955-0095
whaun@becketfund.org
Counsel for Amicus Curiae

1
INTEREST OF THE AMICUS CURIAE1
The Becket Fund for Religious Liberty is a non-profit, nonpartisan law firm 
dedicated to protecting the free expression of all religious traditions. Becket has 
represented agnostics, Buddhists, Christians, Hindus, Jews, Muslims, Santeros, 
Sikhs, and Zoroastrians, among others, in lawsuits across the country. Becket has 
also represented numerous prevailing parties in this Court, including in several 
cases concerning the authority of religious organizations to govern their internal 
affairs and processes without improper government interference. See, e.g., HosannaTabor Evangelical Lutheran Church & Sch. v. EEOC, 565 U.S. 171 (2012); Our Lady 
of Guadalupe Sch. v. Morrissey-Berru, 591 U.S. 732 (2020); Catholic Charities 
Bureau, Inc. v. Wisconsin Lab. & Indus. Rev. Comm’n, 605 U.S. 238 (2025).
Becket submits this brief to clarify how the state court order below undermines
the church autonomy protections this Court has previously recognized. In 
particular, the state court inserted itself into internal religious proceedings by 
ordering Strulovitch to “take all steps necessary” to have the beis din withdraw its 
determination made under Jewish law that Bain has refused to submit to its 
religious authority. Because the harms of the order will be immediate and 
irreparable, this case illustrates why immediate relief can be necessary where 
church autonomy concerns are present. 
1 No counsel for a party authored this brief in whole or in part, and no one other than amicus, its 
members, or its counsel made a monetary contribution to fund the brief’s preparation or submission.

2
INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
Applicants rightly focus on the First Amendment harms to Strulovitch. But there 
is a deeper problem: Absent a stay from this Court, a civil court will cause distinct, 
irreparable, and immediate harm to “a religious body’s right to self-governance.” 
Hosanna-Tabor, 565 U.S. at 201 (Alito, J., joined by Kagan, J., concurring).
“It belongs not to the civil power to enter into or review the proceedings of a 
spiritual court.” Watson v. Jones, 13 Wall. 679, 730 (1872). And yet, a New York trial
court purports to require Strulovitch—under threat of contempt—to keep “disputes
among the parties * * * in front of this Court, and this Court only.” App.009. 
Strulovitch is further ordered to “take all steps necessary to have the Beis Din
withdraw” the seruv, ibid.—a “letter of recalcitrance under Jewish law” issued by a 
religious tribunal to express “religious disapproval,” App.019-020—to “rectify” the 
“damage” to Respondent’s “reputation in the religious community,” App.009. Thus, 
the state court order seeks to reverse a religious determination by a religious
tribunal to control its religious impact. That is a gross violation of the church 
autonomy doctrine, which bars “civil courts” from “disturb[ing] the decisions” of 
“ecclesiastical tribunal[s].” Serbian E. Orthodox Diocese for U.S. of Am. & Canada 
v. Milivojevich, 426 U.S. 696, 709 (1976).
This conclusion follows a long legal tradition recognizing religious institutions 
as “a parallel authority to the state, not a creature of state law.” Catholic Charities,
605 U.S. at 260 (Thomas, J., concurring). Violating that “ancient” principle, 
McRaney v. North Am. Mission Bd., 157 F.4th 627, 634 (5th Cir. 2025), “for even

3
minimal periods of time, unquestionably constitutes irreparable injury,” Mahmoud
v. Taylor, 606 U.S 522, 569 (2025). This Court should grant the stay to preserve the 
autonomy of religious tribunals in New York.
ARGUMENT
I. The Religion Clauses bar civil interference with religious adjudicatory 
systems, including the batei din of New York.
The Religion Clauses guarantee religious groups the “power to decide for 
themselves, free from state interference, matters of church government as well as 
those of faith and doctrine.” Kedroff v. St. Nicholas Cathedral of Russian Orthodox 
Church in N. Am., 344 U.S. 94, 116 (1952). “State interference in that sphere would 
obviously violate the free exercise of religion, and any attempt by government to 
dictate or even to influence such matters would constitute one of the central 
attributes of an establishment of religion.” Our Lady, 591 U.S. at 746. This “general 
principle of church autonomy,” ibid., is part of “[t]he structure of our government,” 
Watson, 13 Wall. at 730, and reflects the “special solicitude” that the Religion Clauses
have for “the rights of religious organizations,” Hosanna-Tabor, 565 U.S. at 189.
In Hosanna-Tabor, this Court unanimously recognized church autonomy as a
structural protection that stops civil courts from adjudicating whether a minister’s 
“threat to sue the Church violated the Synod’s belief that Christians should resolve 
their disputes internally.” 565 U.S. at 180. The Court held that such cases “concern[ ]
government interference with an internal church decision that affects the faith and 
mission of the church itself,” id. at 190, thereby constituting state interference into

4
“a religious body’s right to self-governance,” id. at 201 (Alito, J., joined by Kagan, J.,
concurring). 
Indeed, this Court has repeatedly upheld the principle that “civil courts shall not 
disturb the decisions of the highest ecclesiastical tribunal” in a religious body.
Serbian, 426 U.S. at 709. That has been true since at least 1872, when “Watson [ ]
left civil courts no role to play in reviewing ecclesiastical decisions” made resolving 
religious disputes. Id. at 712 (discussing Watson, 13 Wall. at 727-729). The same
principle was reiterated in Kedroff and Kreshik, where this Court prohibited first
the New York legislature and then the New York courts from transferring authority 
over a New York city cathedral, as doing so contravened “strictly a matter of 
ecclesiastical government.” Kreshik v. St. Nicholas Cathedral, 363 U.S. 190, 190-191
(1960) (discussing Kedroff, 344 U.S. at 116-117). And in Presbyterian Church in U.S.
v. Mary Elizabeth Blue Hull Memorial Presbyterian Church, the Court similarly
prohibited civil courts from “employing religious organizations as an arm of the civil 
judiciary to perform the function of interpreting and applying state standards.” 393 
U.S. 440, 451 (1969). For that same reason, the Court later told the Illinois courts 
in Serbian that they cannot direct the Serbian Orthodox Church to install a different 
person as bishop. 426 U.S. at 698. 
This drumbeat of case law is why lower courts today have no trouble concluding 
that they cannot tell a Lutheran denomination how to organize its polity, Lutheran 
Church—Missouri Synod v. Christian, 178 F.4th 193, 197 (5th Cir. 2026), or punish 
the Russian Orthodox Church Outside of Russia for how it communicated about

5
refusing to elect a bishop, Belya v. Kapral, — F.4th —, 2026 WL 2408741, at *1 (2d 
Cir. Aug. 18, 2026), or second-guess how The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day 
Saints explains tithing to the faithful, Gaddy v. Corp. of the President, 148 F.4th
1202, 1207-1208 (10th Cir. 2025); see also Huntsman v. Corp. of the President, 127 
F.4th 784, 792 (9th Cir. 2025) (Bress, J., concurring) (same); id. at 800 (Bumatay, 
J., concurring). These conclusions are the logical result of the principle underlying
church autonomy: “secular and religious authorities” operate in “distinct spheres.” 
Catholic Charities, 605 U.S. at 258 (Thomas, J., concurring).
This principle should apply with equal force to the batei din of New York. They 
too have “independence” from “state interference” in their decisions on matters 
affecting the faith and mission of Jewish polities. Our Lady, 591 U.S. at 746. But 
here, the New York trial court issued an order purporting to keep this case “in front 
of this Court, and this Court only,” and directing Strulovitch to take “all steps 
necessary to have the Beis Din withdraw” its seruv, “including withdrawing the 
entire proceeding.” App.009. Such an order turns the beis din into a puppet theater, 
with a civil court deciding who says what to the religious tribunal and when. That 
is wildly inconsistent with “the general rule that religious controversies are not the
proper subject of civil court inquiry, and that a civil court must accept the 
ecclesiastical decisions of church tribunals as it finds them.” Serbian, 426 U.S. at 
713. 
Under the trial court’s ruling, Strulovitch is the instrument, but the beis din is 
the target. The trial court’s stated goal in dictating Strulovitch’s actions in a

6
religious court is “rectify[ing] the potential damage to Bain’s reputation in the 
religious community resulting from the issuance of the seruv by the Beis Din,”
App.009. But a state trial court has no authority to countermand the religious
impact of a religious court’s adjudication—and certainly no authority to order
religious actions to undermine it. See Hull, 393 U.S. at 449 (“First Amendment 
values are plainly jeopardized when church property litigation is made to turn on 
the resolution by civil courts of controversies over religious doctrine and practice.”).
Indeed, in a similar case, Judge Kovner rejected a request to enjoin “further 
disseminating” a seruv’s claims. Esses v. Rosen, No. 24-cv-3605, 2024 WL 4494086,
at *2 (E.D.N.Y. Oct. 15, 2024). She did so because “[a]ny implication of impropriety 
in the order of the beth din is plainly made in the context of the Orthodox Jewish 
faith,” “invit[ing] the Court to determine whether a rabbinical court properly applied 
religious principles in disapproving of plaintiff’s conduct.” Id. at *4 (cleaned up). 
Such “judicial intrusion into ecclesiastical doctrine and practice * * * is 
unquestionably forbidden ground under the First Amendment.” Ibid. (cleaned up);
see also Neiman Ginsburg & Mairanz, P.C. v. Goldburd, 684 N.Y.S.2d 405, 407 (N.Y. 
Sup. Ct. 1998) (“[t]his court has no power to review the Beth Din’s determination 
that it was appropriate under Jewish law to issue the seruv,” as this is “a purely 
ecclesiastical question that has been decided by the Beth Din in accordance with 
what it perceives to be Jewish law”). Yet intrusion is exactly what the trial court
ordered below.

7
II. The “neutral principles” approach does not apply to the matters of
internal religious adjudication here.
The New York trial court claimed it could avoid this church autonomy violation 
by applying “neutral principles of secular law to the issues raised herein.” App.008.
Accepting that end-run would eviscerate church autonomy.
The “neutral principles” approach was developed to resolve disputes over formal 
title to church property where competing factions each argued they were the “true” 
church entitled to ownership. See Hull, 393 U.S. at 449. This Court has “never” 
applied it outside that context. McRaney, 157 F.4th at 648; see also LCMS, 178 F.4th
at 201 (noting this “property exception to the church autonomy doctrine is narrow”).
To the contrary, this Court has expressly rejected “reli[ance] on purported ‘neutral 
principles’” to adjudicate matters relating to “internal [church] discipline and 
government.” Serbian, 426 U.S. at 721, 724; see also id. at 715. That’s true even
where, as here, the lower courts claimed they could avoid “determination of 
theological or doctrinal matters.” Id. at 721. Thus, Hosanna-Tabor unanimously 
rejected an invitation to impose “neutral principles” in matters of religious 
governance, recognizing that the purpose of the church autonomy doctrine is to 
prevent ostensibly “neutral” laws from “interfer[ing] with an internal church decision 
that affects the faith and mission of the church itself.” 565 U.S. at 190; cf. Brief for 
the Federal Respondent at 12, 25-27, Hosanna-Tabor, supra (No. 10-553) (urging 
application of “neutral principles” to ministerial selection); Brief for Respondent 
Cheryl Perich at 42-43, Hosanna-Tabor, supra (No. 10-553) (same). A “facially 
‘neutral’ cause[ ] of action” still runs afoul of church autonomy when “application of

8
[its] neutral rules to religious institutions ‘concern[s] government interference’” in 
religious affairs. McRaney, 157 F.4th at 651 (emphasis in original) (quoting HosannaTabor, 565 U.S. at 190)).
The same is true here. Church autonomy simply cannot protect “internal 
management decisions that are essential to the institution’s central mission” if a civil 
court can micromanage the withdrawal of a seruv whenever it disagrees with a beis 
din’s religious decision. Our Lady, 591 U.S. at 746. Cf. Lael Weinberger, The Limits 
of Church Autonomy, 98 Notre Dame L. Rev. 1253, 1277 (2023) (“Neutral 
principles * * * do not provide an outer limit for church autonomy. They eliminate 
church autonomy.”).
III. Gross state interference with religious adjudicatory systems requires
immediate relief. 
Right now, Strulovitch “must,” under court order, return to the beis din and “take 
all steps necessary to have the Beis Din withdraw [its seruv], including withdrawing 
the entire proceeding.” App.009. That order is in place despite the fact that “the [beis 
din] issued [the seruv] of its own volition,” and not on behalf of Strulovitch. App.008.
No other shoe needs to drop. The state court is already interfering in rabbinical court 
proceedings by ordering a participant to seek to alter the rabbinical court’s decision 
on a matter of Jewish law.
In similarly urgent situations, this Court has concluded that interim relief is 
appropriate to prevent civil courts from interfering in religious matters. See 
Mirabelli v. Bonta, 607 U.S. 492, 497 (2026) (per curiam) (granting relief where 
plaintiffs would suffer First Amendment injury “during the potentially protracted

9
appellate process”); Agudath Israel of Am. v. Cuomo, 592 U.S. 1119 (2020) (granting 
relief enjoining COVID occupancy limits on houses of worship); Wheaton Coll. v.
Burwell, 573 U.S. 958 (2014) (per curiam) (granting interim relief to protect college 
from being required to violate its religious beliefs while litigation was pending). That 
is because “the loss of First Amendment freedoms, for even minimal periods of time, 
unquestionably constitutes irreparable injury.” Mahmoud, 606 U.S. at 569 (cleaned 
up). 
Indeed, in the church autonomy context, the need for immediate relief is 
particularly acute—because “the very process” of government intrusion can 
interfere with “rights guaranteed by the Religion Clauses.” NLRB v. Catholic 
Bishop, 440 U.S. 490, 502 (1979); see also Carson v. Makin, 596 U.S. 767, 787 (2022)
(“scrutinizing whether and how” a religious school pursues its mission “raise[s] 
serious concerns about state entanglement with religion”); cf. Yeshiva Univ. v. YU 
Pride All., 143 S. Ct. 1, 2 (2022) (Alito, J., joined by Thomas, Gorsuch, and Barrett, 
JJ., dissenting) (“A State’s imposition of its own mandatory interpretation of 
scripture is a shocking development that calls out for review.”). Here, the ensuing 
harm would be immediate and irreparable, since no later legal judgment could undo
the secular court’s intrusion into the religious affairs of the beis din. This injury 
would unquestionably violate the autonomy of religious organizations in “ordering 
their internal affairs, so that they may be free to * * * define their own doctrines, 
resolve their own disputes, and run their own institutions.” Corporation of Presiding 
Bishop v. Amos, 483 U.S. 327, 341 (1987) (Brennan, J., concurring) (cleaned up).

10
Letting this state interference go unchecked would upend the proper allocation 
of power between civil and religious authority that is part of “the structure of our 
government.” Watson, 13 Wall. at 730. Here, that structure can only be preserved 
by staying the manifestly unconstitutional order of the New York trial court. 
CONCLUSION
The Court should grant the application.
Respectfully submitted.
/s/ William J. Haun
